item.title: Hiroshima Lantern Floating: The Evening of 6 August — Guide
item.description: Every year on the evening of 6 August, after the morning’s memorial ceremony, Hiroshima marks the anniversary of the atomic bombing with toro nagashi, the floating of paper lanterns. Thousands of lanterns, each carrying a handwritten message of peace or remembrance for the dead, are set on the Motoyasu River and drift slowly past the illuminated A-Bomb Dome as darkness falls. It draws people from all over the world and locals whose families were lost that day, and the atmosphere is quiet and profoundly moving rather than festive.

item.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park: A Place of Remembrance — Guide
item.description: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park occupies the open ground near the point where the atomic bomb detonated on 6 August 1945, once a busy commercial district reduced to ash in an instant. Rather than rebuild, the city made it a place of memory and a plea for peace. At its edge stands the A-Bomb Dome, a UNESCO World Heritage Site preserved as a ruin exactly as the blast left it, its skeletal frame one of the most powerful anti-war images in the world.

item.title: Nagasaki Peace Park — Guide
item.description: Nagasaki Peace Park, laid out on a hill near the hypocentre of the atomic bomb dropped on 9 August 1945, is the city’s foremost place of remembrance and its prayer for a world without nuclear weapons. At its heart stands the monumental Peace Statue, a ten-metre bronze figure whose raised right hand points to the threat of nuclear weapons and whose outstretched left hand symbolises peace. Nearby, the Fountain of Peace remembers victims who died desperate for water, and monuments donated by countries around the world line the grounds.

item.title: Kobe Luminarie: Lights of Remembrance — Guide
item.description: Kobe Luminarie is not simply a Christmas illumination. It was created in the winter of 1995, months after the Great Hanshin earthquake killed more than six thousand people and levelled much of the city, as a memorial to the dead and a signal that Kobe would recover. Designed by Italian artists and using techniques from the illuminated festivals of southern Italy, it raises vast arcades and a cathedral-like frontage of hand-painted lightwork over the streets near the old foreign settlement.

item.title: Himeyuri Peace Museum Guide: Access & What to Know
item.description: The Himeyuri Peace Memorial Museum in Itoman, in southern Okinawa, tells one of the most moving stories of the Battle of Okinawa (1945). The “Himeyuri” were a group of around 200 teenage schoolgirls and their teachers mobilised as a student nursing corps; most lost their lives in the final weeks of the battle. The museum and adjacent monument, built where many died, preserve their testimonies, photographs and belongings as a powerful plea for peace.
